concepts.title: Night eyes
concepts.bigIdea: Your night vision sees faint light but almost no color, and it works best when you look slightly to one side.
concepts.bridge: Your night vision is sensitive but nearly colorblind, so faint things look gray and show best when you look a little to one side.

concepts.title: What binoculars add
concepts.bigIdea: Binoculars collect far more light than your pupil, so hundreds of stars you could not see by eye appear.
concepts.bridge: Binoculars gather much more light than your eye can, which is why crowds of extra stars pop into view.

concepts.title: Line of sight
concepts.bigIdea: Stars that look side by side can sit at very different distances; a constellation is a trick of perspective.
concepts.bridge: The sky shows us directions, not depths: two stars that look close together can be very far apart along our line of sight.

concepts.title: How bright it looks
concepts.bigIdea: How bright a star looks depends on how much light it gives out and how far away it is.
concepts.bridge: How bright a star looks depends on two things at once: how much light it really pours out, and how far away it is.

concepts.title: The light-year
concepts.bigIdea: A light-year is a distance: how far light travels in one year.
concepts.bridge: A light-year measures distance, not time: it is how far light gets in one year of travel.

concepts.title: Color is temperature
concepts.bigIdea: A star's color is a thermometer: red-orange stars are the cool ones and blue-white stars are the hot ones.
concepts.bridge: A star's color works like a thermometer: orange-red means a cool surface, blue-white means a hot one.

concepts.title: True power vs looks
concepts.bigIdea: A faint-looking star can be a distant giant, and a bright-looking one can be ordinary and close.
concepts.bridge: Looks deceive: a star can seem faint only because it is far away, while its true power, its luminosity, is enormous.

concepts.title: Looking back in time
concepts.bigIdea: Looking far away means looking back in time, because every object shows you light that left it long ago.
concepts.bridge: Light needs time to cross space, so the farther away something is, the older the view of it you receive.

concepts.title: Stars run on fusion
concepts.bigIdea: Stars shine by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores; they are not fires.
concepts.bridge: Stars are not burning like fires; deep in their cores they fuse hydrogen into helium, and that releases their light.

concepts.title: Sizes of stars
concepts.bigIdea: Stars range from smaller than Earth to wider than Mars's orbit; a star that is cool yet very bright must be huge.
concepts.bridge: Stars come in wildly different sizes, and a star that is cool but still very bright has to be enormous.

concepts.title: Mass is destiny
concepts.bigIdea: Heavy stars live fast and die young and violently; light stars live long and fade quietly.
concepts.bridge: A star's weight decides its life story: heavy stars burn out in a few million years, light ones last for billions.

concepts.title: Star nurseries
concepts.bigIdea: Stars are born in cold clouds of gas and dust, and newborn hot stars make their cloud glow.
concepts.bridge: Stars are born inside cold clouds of gas and dust called nebulae, and the hottest newborns make their cloud glow.

concepts.title: Born in batches
concepts.bigIdea: Stars are born in batches, so a cluster is a family of siblings that all share one birthday.
concepts.bridge: Stars form in batches from one cloud, so an open cluster is a family of siblings with the same birthday.

concepts.title: Reading a cluster's age
concepts.bigIdea: A cluster's brightest remaining stars tell its age: blue giants mean young, and only yellow and orange left means old.
concepts.bridge: In a cluster the heaviest stars die first, so the color of its brightest survivors works like a clock.

concepts.title: Families drift apart
concepts.bigIdea: Clusters slowly dissolve, and their stars spread into loose associations and moving groups that still share a motion.
concepts.bridge: Star families do not stay together forever; they loosen and drift apart, yet their stars keep moving in step.

concepts.title: Giants
concepts.bigIdea: When its core runs out of hydrogen, a star swells into a cool, huge, bright giant.
concepts.bridge: When a star uses up the hydrogen in its core, it swells into a huge, cool and bright red giant.

concepts.title: A gentle ending
concepts.bigIdea: A Sun-like star dies gently: it puffs off its outer layers as a planetary nebula and leaves a white dwarf.
concepts.bridge: A Sun-like star ends quietly: it puffs off its outer layers as a glowing shell and leaves behind a small, hot core, a white dwarf.

concepts.title: A violent ending
concepts.bigIdea: A heavy star ends in a supernova and leaves a neutron star or a black hole.
concepts.bridge: A star far heavier than the Sun ends in a supernova explosion that leaves behind a neutron star or a black hole.

concepts.title: Star stuff
concepts.bigIdea: Dying stars return enriched gas to space, and new stars and planets form from it; we are made of it.
concepts.bridge: Dying stars send gas rich in newly made elements back into space, and later stars and planets, ours included, are built from it.

concepts.title: Double stars
concepts.bigIdea: Many stars are two or more; some are true orbiting pairs, others are chance alignments.
concepts.bridge: Many points of light are really two or more stars; some orbit each other, others only line up by chance.

concepts.title: Weighing stars
concepts.bigIdea: Orbiting pairs let us weigh stars, and that is how we know stellar masses.
concepts.bridge: When two stars orbit each other, the size and pace of the orbit give away their masses; that is how stars are weighed.

concepts.title: Breathing stars
concepts.bigIdea: Some stars swell and shrink and change brightness on a rhythm.
concepts.bridge: Some stars swell and shrink like a slow heartbeat, brightening and fading as they go; astronomers call them variable stars.

concepts.title: Eclipsing pairs
concepts.bigIdea: Some changing stars are really pairs that pass in front of each other.
concepts.bridge: Some stars dim on schedule because a companion we cannot see separately passes in front of them, a tiny regular eclipse.

concepts.title: Cosmic yardsticks
concepts.bigIdea: Stars whose true brightness we know, such as Cepheids, are yardsticks for measuring distance.
concepts.bridge: If you know how bright a light truly is, how faint it looks tells you how far away it is; some pulsing stars reveal their true brightness through their rhythm.

concepts.title: Our galaxy's disk
concepts.bigIdea: The Milky Way band is our galaxy, a flat disk seen edge-on from inside, and nurseries and young clusters crowd along it.
concepts.bridge: The Milky Way band is our own galaxy: a flat disk of stars that we see edge-on because we live inside it.

concepts.title: The ancient halo
concepts.bigIdea: Globular clusters are ancient swarms in a halo around our galaxy's center, and they are older than the Sun.
concepts.bridge: Globular clusters are ancient balls of stars that swarm around our galaxy in a wide halo, well away from its flat disk.

concepts.title: Other galaxies
concepts.bigIdea: Some faint smudges are whole other galaxies, each with billions of stars.
concepts.bridge: Some faint smudges are not clouds or clusters at all but entire galaxies like ours, each holding billions of stars.

concepts.title: The ladder of scale
concepts.bigIdea: From the Sun to stars, clusters, our galaxy and other galaxies, each step out is tens to thousands of times bigger.
concepts.bridge: Each step outward, from stars to clusters to our galaxy to other galaxies, is tens to thousands of times bigger than the last.

concepts.title: The color sequence
concepts.bigIdea: Astronomers sort stars into a temperature sequence, and a star's spectrum also reveals what it is made of.
concepts.bridge: Spread a star's light into a rainbow and dark lines appear; their pattern sorts stars from hottest to coolest and shows what they contain.

concepts.title: Dwarf or giant?
concepts.bigIdea: Two stars of the same color can be a small dwarf and a vast giant; fine details in their light tell which.
concepts.bridge: The same color can belong to a small dwarf or a vast giant; subtle details in the starlight tell the two apart.

concepts.title: Heavier means brighter
concepts.bigIdea: A slightly heavier star shines far more brightly and spends its fuel much faster.
concepts.bridge: A star only a little heavier than another shines far more fiercely, and so it runs through its fuel much sooner.

concepts.title: Spinning stars
concepts.bigIdea: Some stars spin so fast that they bulge at the middle and run hotter at the poles than at the equator.
concepts.bridge: Some stars spin so fast that they flatten into squashed balls, hotter at their poles than around their waists.

concepts.title: Stars with skirts
concepts.bigIdea: Fast-spinning hot stars can fling off a disk of gas that comes and goes, changing their brightness.
concepts.bridge: Very fast-spinning hot stars can shed a ring of gas around their middles, and as it grows and fades their light changes.

concepts.title: Helium-burning giants
concepts.bigIdea: After the first giant phase, stars settle down to burn helium, and many pile up at about the same brightness.
concepts.bridge: After swelling into giants, many stars settle into a calmer stage of burning helium, and they end up remarkably alike in brightness.

concepts.title: Giants shedding skin
concepts.bigIdea: Old giants pulse, cool and lose mass in slow winds, and that gas will later become a planetary nebula.
concepts.bridge: Very old giants pulse and blow off their outer gas in slow winds, the first step toward a planetary nebula.

concepts.title: Sooty red stars
concepts.bigIdea: Late in life some giants dredge freshly made carbon to their surface, and the soot makes them glow deep red.
concepts.bridge: Some ageing giants stir carbon made in their cores up to the surface, and carbon-rich haze turns them a deep red.

concepts.title: Elements made inside
concepts.bigIdea: Some giants show technetium, an element with no stable form, which proves it was made inside the star.
concepts.bridge: Some giants contain an element that decays away and has no stable form, so it must have been forged inside the star itself.

concepts.title: Supergiants' fate
concepts.bigIdea: Stars born with more than about eight times the Sun's mass end their lives as core-collapse supernovae.
concepts.bridge: Supergiants are the heaviest stars nearing their end, and stars like them finish with a supernova when their cores collapse.

concepts.title: The Sun's ember
concepts.bigIdea: The Sun will end as a white dwarf: an Earth-sized ember of carbon and oxygen that slowly cools.
concepts.bridge: A white dwarf is the leftover core of a Sun-like star: about the size of Earth, very dense, and slowly cooling.

concepts.title: A visible black-hole partner
concepts.bigIdea: A blue supergiant you can find in binoculars is orbiting an unseen black hole.
concepts.bridge: When the heaviest stars collapse they can leave black holes, and some of those still orbit a visible partner star.

concepts.title: Stars that steal
concepts.bigIdea: In close pairs one star can pull gas off the other, which turns their life stories upside down.
concepts.bridge: In very close pairs one star can drain gas from its partner, so the lighter star may end up the older-looking one.

concepts.title: Slow giants that fade
concepts.bigIdea: Some cool giants brighten and fade by hundreds of times over about a year.
concepts.bridge: Some cool giants pulse over months, swinging from easy to see to invisible without optics and back again.

concepts.title: Cepheid clocks
concepts.bigIdea: A Cepheid's pulsing rhythm reveals its true brightness, which makes it a cosmic yardstick.
concepts.bridge: Cepheids are pulsing stars whose rhythm gives away how bright they truly are, so they can be used to measure distance.

concepts.title: Halo heartbeats
concepts.bigIdea: Old, light pulsating stars common in globular clusters measure distances across the galaxy's halo.
concepts.bridge: Old, small pulsating stars that beat in less than a day are common in globular clusters and help map our galaxy's halo.

concepts.title: Hidden by soot
concepts.bigIdea: A star can fade dramatically behind soot or dust it has just puffed out.
concepts.bridge: Some stars dim not because they change inside but because they puff out a cloud of dust that briefly hides them.

concepts.title: Stars that flare
concepts.bigIdea: A white dwarf piling up gas stolen from a partner can blow off its surface in a nova, again and again.
concepts.bridge: A nova is a white dwarf that collects gas from a companion until the layer ignites and flares; the star survives and can do it again.

concepts.title: Moving together
concepts.bigIdea: Stars born together keep drifting together across the sky long after their cluster has spread out.
concepts.bridge: Stars born in one family keep sharing the same motion through space even after the family has spread across the sky.

concepts.title: Runaway stars
concepts.bigIdea: Some stars were thrown out of their birth cluster by a supernova or a close encounter and are still fleeing.
concepts.bridge: A runaway star was kicked out of its birth cluster by a close encounter or an exploding partner and is still racing away.

concepts.title: Visitors from the halo
concepts.bigIdea: Some passing stars belong to the galaxy's ancient halo: they are old, poor in heavy elements and fast.
concepts.bridge: A few nearby stars are visitors from our galaxy's old halo, born before much recycled star stuff existed and moving fast.

concepts.title: Stars on the move
concepts.bigIdea: The nearest stars visibly shift across the sky over a human lifetime.
concepts.bridge: Stars are not fixed: the closest ones creep across the sky fast enough to notice within a lifetime.

concepts.title: Our neighbors
concepts.bigIdea: Most of the Sun's nearest neighbors are dim red dwarfs you cannot see without optics.
concepts.bridge: Most stars near the Sun are small, dim red dwarfs, far too faint to see without binoculars.

concepts.title: Suns with planets
concepts.bigIdea: Planets around other stars are common, and some of their host stars are visible in binoculars.
concepts.bridge: Many stars have planets of their own, called exoplanets, found from the tiny tug or dimming they cause.

concepts.title: Dusty belts
concepts.bigIdea: Dusty belts like our own Kuiper belt surround some young nearby stars.
concepts.bridge: Some nearby stars are ringed by belts of dust and rubble, leftovers of planet building like the icy belt beyond Neptune.

concepts.title: The Sun's twins
concepts.bigIdea: Stars almost identical to the Sun show us what our Sun looks like from far away.
concepts.bridge: Some stars are near copies of the Sun, so looking at them shows what our own Sun would look like from far away.

concepts.title: Red stars play tricks
concepts.bigIdea: Red stars seem to brighten the longer you stare at them, which makes judging red variables tricky.
concepts.bridge: Your eye's sensitivity shifts in the dark, so a red star seems to grow brighter the longer you stare; glance, don't stare.

concepts.title: Dust dims and reddens
concepts.bigIdea: Dust between us and a star makes it look fainter and redder than it really is.
concepts.bridge: Space along the Milky Way is laced with dust that dims starlight and tints it redder, like a sunset seen through haze.

concepts.title: Mirrors of dust
concepts.bigIdea: Dust clouds can shine by reflecting nearby starlight, which is why they look blue in photographs.
concepts.bridge: Not every cloud glows on its own; some dust simply reflects nearby starlight, the way fog glows around a streetlight.

concepts.title: Dark clouds
concepts.bigIdea: The dark lanes and holes in the Milky Way are not empty space but dust clouds blocking the stars behind them.
concepts.bridge: Dark patches in the Milky Way are thick dust clouds standing in front of the stars, the raw material for new ones.

concepts.title: Blown bubbles
concepts.bigIdea: The heaviest stars blow fierce winds that inflate glowing bubbles around them before they explode.
concepts.bridge: Very heavy stars blow such strong winds near the end of their lives that they inflate bubbles in the gas around them.

concepts.title: Galaxies in contact
concepts.bigIdea: Galaxies pull on each other, and close encounters can stretch them and set off bursts of star birth.
concepts.bridge: Neighboring galaxies tug on one another, and a close pass can distort them and trigger floods of new stars.

concepts.title: Galaxy companions
concepts.bigIdea: Big galaxies, ours included, are orbited by smaller companion galaxies.
concepts.bridge: Large galaxies have smaller companion galaxies in orbit around them, the way planets have moons.

concepts.title: Along a spiral arm
concepts.bigIdea: Star nurseries and young clusters line up along our galaxy's spiral arms.
concepts.bridge: Our galaxy's disk is wound into spiral arms, and that is where gas piles up and most new stars are born.
